tree_description: Mature 32-inch DBH pine exhibiting a pronounced directional lean toward the residence, placing the home within the tree’s potential failure zone. The tree also exhibits multiple resinous wound areas along the main trunk, consistent with previous injury and localized disruption of the protective bark and underlying woody tissue. Within the upper crown, the main stem transitions into multiple large codominant leaders with narrow attachment unions. These stems constitute a substantial portion of the crown and carry considerable end weight. The overall lean of the tree, combined with the orientation and loading of the upper leaders toward the residence, creates an unfavorable structural configuration and increases concern for leader, stem, or whole-tree failure. The identified defects affect major structural components and cannot be reasonably corrected through conventional pruning without substantially altering the tree's form and canopy. Given the tree's significant lean toward an occupied residence, mature size, trunk wounds, codominant upper-stem architecture, and concentrated loading toward the target, removal is recommended due to the increased potential for significant structural failure and the associated consequences to the adjacent residence.

The tree's directional lean creates additional loading toward the roadway, while the basal defect and compromised root-flare configuration raise concern regarding the tree's ability to adequately support those loads over time. Because the primary defects are located at or immediately adjacent to the base of the tree, they cannot be effectively corrected through pruning or other conventional arboricultural treatment. comments: The February 2021 SOP requires two criteria. This tree meets four: 1. Tip dieback over 30%: An estimated 35–45% of the upper crown is dead, with bare skeletal limbs and full browning during the growing season. 2. Disease: Hypoxylon (Biscogniauxia) canker is present, with black stromata visible on the trunk (see photos). 3. Three or more broken branches 6" or larger: Three separate limb failures have occurred in the past 60 days, each showing internal decay and hollow wood at the break point (see Exhibit B). 4. Extreme mistletoe growth: More than 20 clumps throughout the canopy, with multiple plants on every major branch. Safety concern The recent failures have landed in the most-used parts of the yard: the rear brick patio next to the grill and seating area, and the rear lawn where children play. The attached photos show one limb resting on a planter and another lying across the lawn. Given the decay at the break points, further failures are likely and hard to predict.
